claim: Mutations in Frataxin (FXN) cause Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), a recessive neurodegenerative disorder.
source: Mutations in Frataxin (FXN) cause Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA), a recessive neurodegenerative disorder.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Loss of frataxin homolog (fh) in Drosophila leads to iron toxicity.
source: We show that loss of frataxin homolog (fh) in Drosophila leads to iron toxicity, which in turn induces sphingolipid synthesis and ectopically activates 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase-1 (Pdk1) and myocyte enhancer factor-2 (Mef2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing iron accumulation in fh mutants (Figure 3C and D).

claim: Iron toxicity induces sphingolipid synthesis in fh mutants.
source: We show that loss of frataxin homolog (fh) in Drosophila leads to iron toxicity, which in turn induces sphingolipid synthesis and ectopically activates 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase-1 (Pdk1) and myocyte enhancer factor-2 (Mef2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing increased sphingolipid levels in fh mutants (Figure 5A).

claim: Sphingolipid synthesis ectopically activates Pdk1 and Mef2 in fh mutants.
source: We show that loss of frataxin homolog (fh) in Drosophila leads to iron toxicity, which in turn induces sphingolipid synthesis and ectopically activates 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase-1 (Pdk1) and myocyte enhancer factor-2 (Mef2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing upregulation of Mef2 targets (Figure 6A) and luciferase reporter assays (Figure 6D).

claim: Dampening iron toxicity suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Dampening iron toxicity, inhibiting sphingolipid synthesis by Myriocin, or reducing Pdk1 or Mef2 levels, all effectively suppress neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG data showing improved photoreceptor function with low iron food (Figure 4A) and ferritin overexpression (Figure 4D).

claim: Inhibiting sphingolipid synthesis by Myriocin suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Dampening iron toxicity, inhibiting sphingolipid synthesis by Myriocin, or reducing Pdk1 or Mef2 levels, all effectively suppress neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data showing rescue with Myriocin treatment (Figure 5C).

claim: Reducing Pdk1 levels suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Dampening iron toxicity, inhibiting sphingolipid synthesis by Myriocin, or reducing Pdk1 or Mef2 levels, all effectively suppress neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG data showing rescue with Pdk1 RNAi (Figure 6B).

claim: Reducing Mef2 levels suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Dampening iron toxicity, inhibiting sphingolipid synthesis by Myriocin, or reducing Pdk1 or Mef2 levels, all effectively suppress neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG data showing rescue with Mef2 RNAi (Figure 6B).

claim: Increasing dihydrosphingosine activates Mef2 activity through PDK1 in mammalian neuronal cell line.
source: Moreover, increasing dihydrosphingosine activates Mef2 activity through PDK1 in mammalian neuronal cell line suggesting that the mechanisms are evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay in Neuro-2A cells (Figure 6D).

claim: The iron/sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway mechanisms are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Moreover, increasing dihydrosphingosine activates Mef2 activity through PDK1 in mammalian neuronal cell line suggesting that the mechanisms are evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dhSph activates Mef2 through PDK1 in mammalian cells, similar to fly.

claim: An iron/sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway may play a role in FRDA.
source: Our results indicate that an iron/sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway may play a role in FRDA.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the fly model data and conservation in mammalian cells.

claim: FRDA patients show progressive neurodegeneration of dorsal root ganglia, sensory peripheral nerves, corticospinal tracts, and dentate nuclei of the cerebellum during childhood or early adulthood.
source: During childhood or early adulthood, FRDA patients show a progressive neurodegeneration of dorsal root ganglia, sensory peripheral nerves, corticospinal tracts, and dentate nuclei of the cerebellum (Koeppen, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koeppen, 2011.

claim: FXN is evolutionarily conserved and homologs have been identified in most phyla.
source: FXN is evolutionarily conserved and the homologs have been identified in most phyla (Bencze et al., 2006; Campuzano et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bencze et al., 2006 and Campuzano et al., 1996.

claim: FXN encodes a mitochondrial protein required for iron-sulfur cluster assembly.
source: It encodes a mitochondrial protein that is required for iron-sulfur cluster assembly (Layer et al., 2006; Lill, 2009; Muhlenhoff et al., 2002; Rotig et al., 1997; Yoon and Cowan, 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Iron-sulfur clusters are incorporated into metalloproteins including ETC complexes and aconitase where they function as electron carriers, enzyme catalysts, or regulators of gene expression.
source: Once synthesized, iron-sulfur clusters are incorporated into a variety of metalloproteins, including proteins of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and aconitase, where they function as electron carriers, enzyme catalysts, or regulators of gene expression (Lill, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lill, 2009.

claim: Loss of FXN leads to impaired ETC complex which triggers ROS production that directly contributes to cellular toxicity.
source: It has been proposed that loss of FXN leads to impaired ETC complex, which in turn triggers ROS production that directly contributes to cellular toxicity (Al-Mahdawi et al., 2006; Anderson et al., 2008; Calabrese et al., 2005; Schulz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The ROS hypothesis for FRDA pathogenesis has been questioned in several studies.
source: However, the ROS hypothesis has been questioned in several studies.
evidence: Supported by subsequent citations showing limited ROS effects.

claim: Loss of FXN only leads to modest hypersensitivity to oxidative stress.
source: For example, loss of FXN only leads to a modest hypersensitivity to oxidative stress (Macevilly and Muller, 1997; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Several clinical trials based on antioxidant therapy in FRDA patients have shown no or limited benefits.
source: In addition, several clinical trails based on antioxidant therapy in FRDA patients have shown no or limited benefits (Lynch et al., 2010; Parkinson et al., 2013; Santhera Pharmaceuticals, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trial reports.

claim: Loss of yeast frataxin homolog results in iron accumulation.
source: Loss of yeast frataxin homolog results in iron accumulation (Babcock et al., 1997), and this phenotype has also been reported in cardiac muscles of a Fxn deficiency mouse and FRDA patients (Koeppen, 2011; Lamarche et al., 1980; Michael et al., 2006; Puccio et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Iron accumulation has been reported in cardiac muscles of Fxn deficiency mouse and FRDA patients.
source: Loss of yeast frataxin homolog results in iron accumulation (Babcock et al., 1997), and this phenotype has also been reported in cardiac muscles of a Fxn deficiency mouse and FRDA patients (Koeppen, 2011; Lamarche et al., 1980; Michael et al., 2006; Puccio et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Whether iron accumulates in the nervous system upon loss of FXN remains controversial.
source: However, whether iron accumulates in the nervous system upon loss of FXN remains controversial.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by conflicting citations.

claim: Elevated iron levels were observed in the dentate nuclei or in glia cells of FRDA patients.
source: It has been reported that elevated iron levels were observed in the dentate nuclei or in glia cells of FRDA patients (Boddaert et al., 2007; Koeppen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boddaert et al., 2007 and Koeppen et al., 2012.

claim: There is no increase of iron in the nervous system of Fxn deficiency mice and FRDA patients according to some studies.
source: Contrary to these results, others suggested that there is no increase of iron in the nervous system of Fxn deficiency mice and FRDA patients (Koeppen et al., 2007; Puccio et al., 2001; Solbach et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The first mutant allele of fh was identified in an unbiased forward genetic screen aimed at isolating mutations that cause neurodegenerative phenotypes.
source: We identified the first mutant allele of fh in an unbiased forward genetic screen aimed at isolating mutations that cause neurodegenerative phenotypes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach used.

claim: Loss of fh causes age dependent neurodegeneration in photoreceptors.
source: We show that loss of fh causes an age dependent neurodegeneration in photoreceptors and affects mitochondrial function.
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data over time (Figure 1A and B).

claim: Loss of fh affects mitochondrial function.
source: We show that loss of fh causes an age dependent neurodegeneration in photoreceptors and affects mitochondrial function.
evidence: Supported by ETC complex activity and ATP production data (Figure 2B and C).

claim: Unlike other mitochondrial mutants with impaired ETC activity, fh mutants do not show an increase in ROS.
source: Unlike other mitochondrial mutants with impaired ETC activity, we do not observe an increase in ROS.
evidence: Supported by DHE staining data (Figure 2D).

claim: Loss of fh causes iron accumulation in the nervous system.
source: However, loss of fh causes an iron accumulation in the nervous system, induces an up-regulation of sphingolipid synthesis, and activation of Pdk1 and Mef2.
evidence: Supported by RPA and Perls' staining data (Figure 3C and D).

claim: Loss of fh induces up-regulation of sphingolipid synthesis.
source: However, loss of fh causes an iron accumulation in the nervous system, induces an up-regulation of sphingolipid synthesis, and activation of Pdk1 and Mef2.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 5A).

claim: Loss of fh causes activation of Pdk1 and Mef2.
source: However, loss of fh causes an iron accumulation in the nervous system, induces an up-regulation of sphingolipid synthesis, and activation of Pdk1 and Mef2.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing upregulation of Mef2 targets (Figure 6A).

claim: Reducing iron toxicity significantly suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Reducing iron toxicity or inhibiting the sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway significantly suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG data with low iron food and ferritin overexpression (Figure 4A and D).

claim: Inhibiting the sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway significantly suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Reducing iron toxicity or inhibiting the sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway significantly suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG data with Myriocin treatment and Pdk1/Mef2 RNAi (Figures 5C and 6B).

claim: This is the first evidence that sphingolipids, Pdk1, and Mef2 play a primary role in FXN-induced neurodegeneration.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that sphingolipids, Pdk1, and the transcription factor Mef2 are shown to play a primary role in FXN-induced neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a claim about novelty based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The molecular lesion in fh mutants is S136R in a highly conserved region required for FXN binding to the iron-sulfur cluster assembly complex.
source: The molecular lesion, S136R, is in a highly conserved region, which is required for the FXN binding to the iron-sulfur cluster assembly complex (Tsai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2011 and sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Six point mutations adjacent to S136 (S157 in human) have been reported in FRDA patients.
source: In addition, six point mutations adjacent to S136 (S157 in human) have been reported in FRDA patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Santos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2010 and sequence alignment figure.

claim: Hemizygous fh mutants are L3 to pupal lethal.
source: Hemizygous fh mutants are L3 to pupal lethal, and the lethality is not enhanced in transheterozygous mutants that carry a deficiency (fh/Df (1)BSC537), suggesting that S136R is a severe loss-of-function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lethal phase analysis data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: S136R is a severe loss-of-function mutation.
source: Hemizygous fh mutants are L3 to pupal lethal, and the lethality is not enhanced in transheterozygous mutants that carry a deficiency (fh/Df (1)BSC537), suggesting that S136R is a severe loss-of-function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of enhanced lethality in transheterozygous mutants.

claim: The lethality of fh can be rescued by a genomic fh construct.
source: The lethality of fh can be rescued by a genomic fh construct (gfh), or by ubiquitous expression (da-GAL4 driver) of fh cDNA using the UAS/GAL4 system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lethal phase analysis data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The lethality of fh can be rescued by ubiquitous expression of fh cDNA using the UAS/GAL4 system.
source: The lethality of fh can be rescued by a genomic fh construct (gfh), or by ubiquitous expression (da-GAL4 driver) of fh cDNA using the UAS/GAL4 system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lethal phase analysis data and citation to Brand and Perrimon, 1993.

claim: The lethality of fh cannot be rescued with tissue specific drivers including neuronal, muscular, or glial drivers.
source: The lethality cannot be rescued with tissue specific drivers, including neuronal (nSyb-GAL4), muscular (Mef2-GAL4), or glial (repo-GAL4) drivers, suggesting a requirement for fh in multiple tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lethal phase analysis data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: fh is required in multiple tissues.
source: The lethality cannot be rescued with tissue specific drivers, including neuronal (nSyb-GAL4), muscular (Mef2-GAL4), or glial (repo-GAL4) drivers, suggesting a requirement for fh in multiple tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the inability of tissue-specific rescue to prevent lethality.

claim: fh mutants exhibit a smaller body size and prolonged larval stages (10 to 12 days instead of 5 days for wild type animals).
source: In addition, fh mutants exhibit a smaller body size and prolonged larval stages (10 to 12 days instead of 5 days for wild type animals), similar to other mitochondrial mutants (Sandoval et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, compared to other mitochondrial mutants via citations.

claim: Removal of maternal wild type fh mRNA or protein in the egg exacerbates the lethal phase from pupal to embryonic lethality.
source: Interestingly, removal of maternal wild type fh mRNA or protein in the egg exacerbates the lethal phase from pupal to embryonic lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lethal phase analysis data with OvoD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Residual maternally deposited wild type Fh extends the lifespan and creates a partial loss of Fh condition in fh mutants.
source: In essence, the residual maternally deposited wild type Fh not only extends the lifespan but also creates a partial loss of Fh condition in the fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that removing maternal Fh causes earlier lethality.

claim: ERG amplitudes of newly eclosed fh mutants (Day 1) are ~60% of control animals.
source: In response to a light stimulus, the ERG amplitudes of newly eclosed fh mutants (Day 1) are ~60% of control animals (y,w,FRT19Aiso, the isogenized flies used in the screen) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ERG recording data (Figure 1A).

claim: ERG amplitudes of fh mutants rapidly decline over a six day period.
source: The ERG amplitudes rapidly decline over a six day period (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ERG recording data over time (Figure 1A).

claim: fh mutant clones contain a normal number of photoreceptors with typical trapezoidal organization at Day 1.
source: Morphologically, the fh mutant clones contain a normal number of photoreceptors with a typical trapezoidal organization at Day 1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 1B).

claim: Day 1 fh mutant photoreceptors exhibit expansion of the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: However, by using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we found that Day 1 fh mutant photoreceptors exhibit an expansion of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and a dramatic accumulation of lipid droplets in glial cells that are not observed in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by TEM data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Day 1 fh mutant photoreceptors exhibit dramatic accumulation of lipid droplets in glial cells.
source: However, by using transmission electron microscopy (TEM), we found that Day 1 fh mutant photoreceptors exhibit an expansion of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and a dramatic accumulation of lipid droplets in glial cells that are not observed in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by TEM data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).

claim: At Day 3, photoreceptors in fh mutant clones exhibit aberrant elongated rhabdomeres.
source: At Day 3, photoreceptors in mutant clones exhibit aberrant elongated rhabdomeres (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 1B).

claim: By Day 6, many photoreceptors are missing in fh mutant clones, whereas control retinas exhibit intact morphology.
source: By Day 6, many of the photoreceptors are missing in the mutant clones, whereas control retinas exhibit intact morphology (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and TEM imaging (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: The neurodegeneration in fh mutants can be fully rescued by a genomic fh construct.
source: The neurodegeneration can be fully rescued by a genomic fh construct or by expressing fh cDNA in photoreceptors (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that photoreceptor degeneration is cell-autonomous.
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: The neurodegeneration in fh mutants can be fully rescued by expressing fh cDNA in photoreceptors.
source: The neurodegeneration can be fully rescued by a genomic fh construct or by expressing fh cDNA in photoreceptors (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that photoreceptor degeneration is cell-autonomous.
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Photoreceptor degeneration in fh mutants is cell-autonomous.
source: The neurodegeneration can be fully rescued by a genomic fh construct or by expressing fh cDNA in photoreceptors (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that photoreceptor degeneration is cell-autonomous.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of photoreceptor-specific rescue to prevent degeneration.

claim: Expression of human FXN cDNA rescues neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Moreover, expression of the human FXN cDNA rescues neurodegeneration in fh mutants (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), showing that fly and human FXN have conserved molecular function, and that our studies are relevant to the biological role of human FXN.
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Fly and human FXN have conserved molecular function.
source: Moreover, expression of the human FXN cDNA rescues neurodegeneration in fh mutants (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), showing that fly and human FXN have conserved molecular function, and that our studies are relevant to the biological role of human FXN.
evidence: Inferred from the functional rescue by human FXN in fly mutants.

claim: FXN has been reported to be localized to mitochondria.
source: FXN has been reported to be localized to mitochondria (Koutnikova et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koutnikova et al., 1997.

claim: Fh colocalizes with mitoGFP in larval motor neuron.
source: Indeed, Fh colocalizes with mitoGFP in larval motor neuron, and removing the predicted mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) of fh cDNA (Fh-∆MTS-V5) leads to a diffused signal in the cytosol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Removing the predicted mitochondrial targeting sequence of fh cDNA leads to a diffused signal in the cytosol.
source: Indeed, Fh colocalizes with mitoGFP in larval motor neuron, and removing the predicted mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) of fh cDNA (Fh-∆MTS-V5) leads to a diffused signal in the cytosol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Removal of the MTS leads to a dysfunctional Fh protein.
source: Removal of the MTS leads to a dysfunctional protein as expression of Fh-∆MTS-V5 in the fh mutant clone is not able to rescue the ERG defect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ERG data showing lack of rescue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Loss of fh causes highly aberrant mitochondrial morphology in one day old adult photoreceptors.
source: Loss of fh causes a highly aberrant mitochondrial morphology in one day old adult photoreceptors.
evidence: Supported by TEM data (Figure 2A).

claim: Mitochondria in fh mutants are larger and exhibit aberrant cristae and altered inner membrane morphology.
source: The mitochondria in fh mutants are larger and exhibit aberrant cristae and altered inner membrane morphology (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by TEM data (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Loss of FXN has been reported to cause various ETC and respiratory defects in different animal models.
source: Loss of FXN has been reported to cause various ETC and respiratory defects in different animal models, including yeast, fly, mouse, as well as FRDA patients (Al-Mahdawi et al., 2006; Anderson et al., 2005; Carletti et al., 2014; Koutnikova et al., 1997; Puccio et al., 2001; Rotig et al., 1997; Wilson and Roof, 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: ETC Complex I activity is severely reduced in fh mutants when compared to control and genomic rescued animals.
source: We find that ETC Complex I (CI) activity is severely reduced in fh mutants when compared to control and genomic rescued animals (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ETC complex activity assay data (Figure 2B).

claim: The ADP/ATP ratio is increased in fh mutants.
source: Consistent with this data, the ADP/ATP ratio is increased in fh mutants (Figure 2C), showing that energy production is impaired.
evidence: Supported by ADP/ATP ratio assay data (Figure 2C).

claim: Energy production is impaired in fh mutants.
source: Consistent with this data, the ADP/ATP ratio is increased in fh mutants (Figure 2C), showing that energy production is impaired.
evidence: Inferred from the increased ADP/ATP ratio.

claim: Impaired ETC CI activity has been linked to increased ROS production.
source: Impaired ETC CI activity has been linked to increased ROS production that in turn causes cellular stress or toxicity (Sugioka et al., 1988; Turrens and Boveris, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sugioka et al., 1988 and Turrens and Boveris, 1980.

claim: Neuronal down-regulation of ND42 exhibits strong DHE fluorescence in the larval ventral nerve cord, indicating elevated levels of ROS.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, loss of ND42 exhibits strong DHE fluorescence in the larval ventral nerve cord, indicating elevated levels of ROS.
evidence: Supported by DHE staining data (Figure 2D).

claim: DHE levels are not obviously increased in fh mutants, suggesting no or a very mild increase in ROS.
source: However, DHE levels are not obviously increased in fh mutants, suggesting no or a very mild increase in ROS (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by DHE staining data (Figure 2D).

claim: Overexpression of ROS scavengers (Catalase, SOD1, SOD2) does not suppress neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Consistent with the DHE data, overexpression of these ROS scavengers does not suppress neurodegeneration in fh mutants (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with ROS scavenger overexpression (Figure 2E).

claim: Feeding fh mutants with AD4, a potent antioxidant, does not suppress neurodegeneration.
source: Furthermore, feeding fh mutants with AD4, a potent antioxidant that dampens oxidative stress (Amer et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2015), does not suppress neurodegeneration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with AD4 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: ROS does not contribute to the demise of neurons in fh mutants.
source: Taken together, our findings argue that ROS does not contribute to the demise of neurons in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increased ROS and lack of rescue by ROS scavengers.

claim: Knockdown of fh in flies causes lipid droplet accumulation in glia.
source: It has been proposed that lipid droplets play a role in the pathogenesis of FRDA as knockdown of fh in flies causes lipid droplet accumulation in glia (Navarro et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Navarro et al., 2010.

claim: Strong lipid droplet accumulation is observed in glial cells of fh mutant clones.
source: From TEM and nile red staining, we observed a strong lipid droplet accumulation in glial cells of fh mutant clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by TEM and nile red staining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: The level of JNK pathway reporter puc-lacZ is not altered in fh mutants.
source: However, we do not observe elevated ROS levels (Figure 2D), and the level of a JNK pathway reporter, puc-lacZ, is not altered in fh mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging of puc-lacZ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Overexpression of brummer lipase or lipase 4 effectively reduces the number of lipid droplets but does not delay neurodegeneration of fh mutants.
source: Finally, overexpression of brummer lipase (Bmm) or lipase 4 (lip4), homologs of human Adipose Triglyceride Lipase (ATGL) or acid lipase (Gronke et al., 2005) respectively, effectively reduces the number of lipid droplet but does not delay neurodegeneration of fh mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that these lipid droplets do not contribute to neurodegeneration.
evidence: Supported by nile red staining and ERG data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Lipid droplets do not contribute to neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Finally, overexpression of brummer lipase (Bmm) or lipase 4 (lip4), homologs of human Adipose Triglyceride Lipase (ATGL) or acid lipase (Gronke et al., 2005) respectively, effectively reduces the number of lipid droplet but does not delay neurodegeneration of fh mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that these lipid droplets do not contribute to neurodegeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of rescue when lipid droplets are reduced.

claim: Some mitochondrial mutants display activity dependent degeneration of photoreceptors.
source: We recently discovered that some mutants that are required for mitochondrial function display an activity dependent degeneration of photoreceptors (Jaiswal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaiswal et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondrial mutants share common phenotypes including reduced ATP production, ERG rundown upon repetitive stimulation, and Rh1 accumulation upon light exposure.
source: These mitochondrial mutants share several common phenotypes, including reduced ATP production, ERG rundown upon repetitive stimulation, and Rhodopsin1 (Rh1) accumulation in the photoreceptor cytoplasm upon light exposure (Jaiswal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaiswal et al., 2015.

claim: Dysfunctional mitochondria cause reduced ATP production and decreased calcium influx, leading to reduced photoreceptor depolarization and Rh1 internalization.
source: In these mutants, dysfunctional mitochondria cause reduced ATP production and decreased calcium influx, which not only leads to reduced photoreceptor depolarization, but also triggers an internalization of Rh1 leading to an overload of the endolysosomal system upon light stimulation (Jaiswal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaiswal et al., 2015.

claim: The accumulation of Rh1 results in activity dependent degeneration.
source: The accumulation of Rh1 results in activity dependent degeneration, as the photoreceptors only degenerate when flies are raised in light (light-induced neuronal activity) but not in dark (no neuronal activity) (Alloway et al., 2000; Chinchore et al., 2009; Jaiswal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The ERG amplitude rapidly declines during repetitive light stimulation in fh mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the ERG amplitudes of the first and last traces show a similar size in control animals. In contrast, the ERG amplitude rapidly declines during repetitive light stimulation in fh mutants (Figure 3A), similar to other mitochondrial mutants (Jaiswal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with repetitive stimulation (Figure 3A).

claim: Rh1 accumulates in the cytoplasm of fh mutant photoreceptors upon light exposure.
source: Wild type flies exposed to 12 hr of constant light typically exhibit low levels of Rh1 in photoreceptors (Figure 3B). However, in fh mutants, Rh1 accumulates in the cytoplasm of photoreceptors (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging of Rh1 (Figure 3B).

claim: fh mutant flies raised in the dark still display severe photoreceptor degeneration.
source: However, fh mutant flies that are raised in the dark still display severe photoreceptor degeneration (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by ERG data in dark conditions (Figure 3B).

claim: Another pathogenic mechanism in addition to Rh1 accumulation contributes to neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Hence, we propose that in addition to the Rh1 accumulation, another pathogenic mechanism must contribute to neurodegeneration and mask the rescue effect when flies are raised in dark.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dark rearing does not prevent degeneration.

claim: The RPA intensity in fh mutants is dramatically reduced in both muscle and NMJ boutons, suggesting strong Fe2+ accumulation in mitochondria.
source: In fh mutants rescued with the genomic fh, which serves as a negative control, the RPA signal exhibits strong fluorescence (Figure 3C). In contrast, the RPA intensity in fh mutants is dramatically reduced, in both muscle and NMJ boutons, suggesting a strong Fe2+ accumulation in mitochondria (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by RPA staining data (Figure 3C).

claim: RPAC fluorescence is not quenched in rescued animals and fh mutants, suggesting that decreased RPA fluorescence in fh mutants is not due to impaired dye uptake.
source: RPAC (Rhodamine B-((phenanthren-9-yl)-aminocarbonyl) benzyl ester), a dye that is structurally very similar to RPA, is also taken up by mitochondria but is insensitive to Fe2+ mediated fluorescence quenching. Indeed, RPAC fluorescence is not quenched in rescued animals (fh; gfh) and fh mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the decreased fluorescence of RPA in fh mutants is not due to impaired dye uptake.
evidence: Supported by RPAC staining data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The DAB signal is dramatically increased in fh mutants, indicating that loss of fh leads to severe accumulation of Fe3+.
source: In control and rescued animals, the DAB signal is most obvious in the neuropil of the ventral nerve cord (Figure 3D), suggesting that Fe3+ is unevenly distributed in the nervous system. In fh mutants, however, the DAB signal is dramatically increased (Figure 3D), indicating that loss of fh leads to a severe accumulation of Fe3+.
evidence: Supported by Perls'/DAB staining data (Figure 3D).

claim: Increased Fe3+ levels are found in the larval brain, fat body, and gut of fh mutants.
source: Increased Fe3+ levels are not only found in the larval brain, but can also be observed in fat body and gut (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Loss of fh leads to both Fe2+ and Fe3+ accumulation in multiple tissues, including the nervous system.
source: Together, these results indicate that loss of fh leads to both Fe2+ and Fe3+ accumulation in multiple tissues, including the nervous system.
evidence: Inferred from the RPA and Perls'/DAB staining data.

claim: Feeding larvae with low iron food reduces iron levels in the brains of both wild type control and fh mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, feeding larvae with low iron food reduces iron levels in the brains of both wild type control and fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by Perls'/DAB staining data with low iron food (Figure 3D).

claim: The lethal phase of fh mutants is susceptible to iron levels in the food.
source: In addition, the lethal phase of fh mutants is susceptible to iron levels in the food.
evidence: Supported by pupation rate data with different iron concentrations (Figure 3E).

claim: In low iron food, 80% of fh mutants develop into pupae, but addition of 10 mM Fe3+ reduces pupation to about 10%.
source: In low iron food, 80% of fh mutants develop into pupae, but addition of 10 mM Fe3+ to the low iron food reduces pupation to about 10%, whereas the pupation rate of controls is not affected (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by pupation rate data (Figure 3E).

claim: fh mutants are highly sensitive to iron levels.
source: These data indicate that fh mutants are highly sensitive to iron levels.
evidence: Inferred from the pupation rate data showing iron-dependent lethality.

claim: Treating fh mutants with low iron food improves the ERG defects when compared to regular food condition.
source: To determine if iron toxicity is underlying the observed neurodegeneration, we fed low iron food to fh mutants and examined photoreceptor degeneration. Treating fh mutants with low iron food improves the ERG defects when compared to regular food condition (Figure 4A), suggesting that iron mediated toxicity contributes to neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by ERG data with low iron food (Figure 4A).

claim: Iron mediated toxicity contributes to neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: Treating fh mutants with low iron food improves the ERG defects when compared to regular food condition (Figure 4A), suggesting that iron mediated toxicity contributes to neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the improvement in ERG with low iron food.

claim: Reducing photoreceptor activity (raising flies in dark) and iron (low iron food) leads to a synergistic effect in restoring both photoreceptor function and morphology in fh mutants.
source: Interestingly, reducing photoreceptor activity (raising flies in dark) and iron (low iron food) leads to a synergistic effect in restoring both photoreceptor function and morphology (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data with combined dark and low iron conditions (Figure 4A and B).

claim: Reintroducing iron into low iron food induces rapid degeneration in fh mutant clones even when animals are raised in dark.
source: To exclude the possibility that changes in other compounds than iron in low iron food suppresses neurodegeneration in fh mutants, we reintroduced iron into the low iron food (low iron/10 mM iron) and found that this treatment again induces rapid degeneration in fh mutant clones even when animals are raised in dark (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by morphological and ERG data with iron supplementation (Figure 4B and C).

claim: Iron toxicity contributes to activity independent degeneration in fh mutants.
source: These data suggest that iron toxicity contributes to the activity independent degeneration, as photoreceptors degenerate in the absence of neuronal activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that photoreceptors degenerate in dark with high iron.

claim: Co-expression of Fer1HCH and Fer2LCH significantly suppresses degeneration in fh mutant clones when flies are raised in dark.
source: In fh mutant clones, co-expression of Fer1HCH and Fer2LCH (fh; Rh1>Fer1, Fer2) or expression of Fer3HCH alone (fh; Rh1>Fer3) significantly suppresses degeneration when flies are raised in dark (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with ferritin overexpression (Figure 4D).

claim: Expression of Fer3HCH alone significantly suppresses degeneration in fh mutant clones when flies are raised in dark.
source: In fh mutant clones, co-expression of Fer1HCH and Fer2LCH (fh; Rh1>Fer1, Fer2) or expression of Fer3HCH alone (fh; Rh1>Fer3) significantly suppresses degeneration when flies are raised in dark (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with ferritin overexpression (Figure 4D).

claim: Co-expression of ferroxidase inactive form of Fer1HCH along with wild type Fer2LCH in fh mutants did not rescue degeneration.
source: Co-expression of a ferroxidase inactive form of Fer1HCH along with wild type Fer2LCH in fh mutants (fh; Rh1>Fer1*, Fer2) did not rescue degeneration (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with inactive ferritin (Figure 4D).

claim: Excess neuronal activity (activity dependent) and accumulated iron (activity independent) synergize to promote photoreceptor degeneration in fh mutants.
source: In summary, we conclude that excess neuronal activity (activity dependent) and accumulated iron (activity independent) synergize to promote photoreceptor degeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects of light/dark and iron conditions on degeneration.

claim: Wild type yeast grown in medium with high iron levels increases sphingolipid synthesis.
source: It has been previously documented that wild type yeast grow in medium with high iron levels increases sphingolipid synthesis (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: This phenotype (increased sphingolipid synthesis with high iron) was not documented in yeast frataxin homolog mutants or FXN mutants in other organisms.
source: However, this phenotype was not documented in the yeast frataxin homolog mutants or FXN mutants in other organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior documentation in the literature.

claim: Several upstream metabolic intermediates of sphingolipids are increased in fh mutants.
source: Consistent to our hypothesis, several upstream metabolic intermediates of sphingolipids are increased in fh mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 5A).

claim: Dihydrosphingosine is increased more than 10 fold in fh mutants.
source: Strikingly, dihydrosphingosine (dhSph) is increased more than 10 fold in fh mutants.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 5A).

claim: Dihydroceramide and sphingosine are increased to different levels in fh mutants.
source: Other sphingolipids, such as dihydroceramide (dhCer) and sphingosine (Sph), are also increased to different levels (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 5A).

claim: The de novo synthesis of sphingolipids is increased in fh mutants.
source: This data suggest that the de novo synthesis of sphingolipids is increased in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the increased levels of sphingolipid intermediates.

claim: RNAi mediated knockdown of lace significantly improved the ERG defects of fh mutants.
source: To determine if increased sphingolipid synthesis contributes to neurodegeneration in fh mutants, we performed RNAi experiments against the first and rate-limiting enzyme in the de novo synthesis pathway, lace, the fly homolog of Serine palmitoyltransferase. This significantly improved the ERG defects of fh mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with lace RNAi (Figure 5B).

claim: Feeding fh mutants Myriocin suppressed both functional and morphological photoreceptor defects.
source: In addition, feeding fh mutants Myriocin, a serine palmitoyltransferase inhibitor, suppressed both the functional and morphological photoreceptor defects of fh mutant clones (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data with Myriocin treatment (Figure 5C).

claim: Low iron food and myriocin treatment do not show an additive or synergistic effect in fh mutants.
source: To assess if iron accumulation and increased sphingolipid synthesis act in the same or a different pathway, we treated fh mutants with low iron food as well as myriocin. As shown in Figure 5D, we did not observe an additive or synergistic effect.
evidence: Supported by ERG data with combined treatments (Figure 5D).

claim: Iron toxicity induces sphingolipid synthesis which causes neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
source: These results suggest that iron toxicity induces sphingolipid synthesis which in turn causes neurodegeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of additive effect between iron reduction and sphingolipid inhibition.

claim: Increased sphingolipids in yeast activate a kinase pathway (Pkh1/Ypk1/Smp1) that converges on transcription factor Smp1p.
source: Increased sphingolipids in yeast have been shown to activate a kinase pathway (Pkh1/Ypk1/Smp1) that converges on a transcription factor Smp1p (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: This pathway (Pkh1/Ypk1/Smp1) has not yet been studied in higher eukaryotic cells or FXN mutant animal models.
source: However, this pathway has not yet been studied in higher eukaryotic cells, or FXN mutant animal models.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior studies in the literature.

claim: The corresponding proteins to yeast Pkh1/Ypk1/Smp1 in mammals are PDK1, SGK, and Mef2 transcription factor.
source: The corresponding proteins in mammals are PDK1, SGK (serum- and glucocorticoid regulated kinase), and Mef2 transcription factor (Casamayor et al., 1999; Dodou and Treisman, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Casamayor et al., 1999 and Dodou and Treisman, 1997.

claim: Mef2 is expressed in certain neurons and photoreceptors.
source: The MEFs are also expressed in neurons where they are involved in neuronal development (Akhtar et al., 2012; Leifer et al., 1994; Lyons et al., 1995; Mao et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Seven Mef2 targets are all ectopically expressed in response to ectopic expression of Mef2 in vivo.
source: Seven Mef2 targets, which have been validated through in situ hybridization and qRT-PCR, are all ectopically expressed in response to ectopic expression of Mef2 in vivo (Elgar et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elgar et al., 2008.

claim: All seven Mef2 targets are up-regulated in the nervous system of fh mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, all of these Mef2 targets are up-regulated.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 6A).

claim: Several negative control genes are not changed in fh mutants.
source: Several negative control genes, the downstream targets of other transcription factors, including Enhancer of split (E(Spl)), senseless (sens), and patched (ptc), as well as several housekeeping genes that are not Mef2 targets (Sandmann et al., 2006), are not changed in fh mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Mef2 is abnormally activated in fh mutants.
source: These data indicate that Mef2 is abnomally activated in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the upregulation of Mef2 target genes.

claim: RNAi mediated knockdown of Pdk1 suppresses the ERG and morphological defects in fh mutants.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, RNAi mediated knockdown of Pdk1 suppresses the ERG and morphological defects in fh mutants (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data with Pdk1 RNAi (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Knock down of Mef2 by two independent RNAi lines suppresses neurodegeneration of fh mutants.
source: Furthermore, knock down of Mef2 by two independent RNAi lines suppresses neurodegeneration of fh mutants (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that activated Pdk1 and Mef2 are toxic and contribute to the degeneration.
evidence: Supported by ERG and morphological data with Mef2 RNAi (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Activated Pdk1 and Mef2 are toxic and contribute to degeneration in fh mutants.
source: Furthermore, knock down of Mef2 by two independent RNAi lines suppresses neurodegeneration of fh mutants (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that activated Pdk1 and Mef2 are toxic and contribute to the degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue by Pdk1 and Mef2 knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of Mef2 in wild type photoreceptors is sufficient to induce neurodegeneration.
source: To determine if up-regulation of Mef2 in wild type photoreceptors is sufficient to induce neurodegeneration, we ectopically expressed Mef2 in the adult eye using Rh1-Gal4. Overexpression of Mef2 is sufficient to cause photoreceptor degeneration (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ERG data with Mef2 overexpression (Figure 6C).

claim: Flies with neuronal expression of Mef2 die within a week, instead of 70–80 days of wild type flies.
source: Furthermore, flies with neuronal expression of Mef2 (nSyb>Mef2) die within a week, instead of 70–80 days of the wild type flies (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Abnormal activation of Mef2 in neuron is sufficient to trigger its demise.
source: These data suggest that abnormal activation of Mef2 in neuron is sufficient to trigger its demise.
evidence: Inferred from the lethality and degeneration caused by Mef2 overexpression.

claim: dhSph induces luciferase signals of a Mef2 reporter in a concentration dependent manner in Neuro-2A cells.
source: dhSph, the sphingolipid that is increased more than 10 fold in fly fh mutants (Figure 5A), induces luciferase signals of a Mef2 reporter in a concentration dependent manner (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data (Figure 6D).

claim: The increased luciferase signal from dhSph is suppressed by adding the PDK1 inhibitor GSK2334470 in Neuro-2A cells.
source: In addition, the increased luciferase signal is suppressed by adding the PDK1 inhibitor GSK2334470 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data with PDK1 inhibitor (Figure 6D).

claim: dhSph activates Mef2 through PDK1 in mammalian cells.
source: This data indicate that dhsph activates Mef2 through PDK1, consistent with what we observed in the fly.
evidence: Inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results with dhSph and PDK1 inhibitor.

claim: Sphingolipids act as signaling molecules to activate the Pdk1/Mef2 pathway.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that sphingolipids act as signaling molecules to activate the Pdk1/Mef2 pathway and that this pathway contributes to photoreceptor degeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the combined genetic and cell culture data.

claim: The Pdk1/Mef2 pathway contributes to photoreceptor degeneration in fh mutants.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that sphingolipids act as signaling molecules to activate the Pdk1/Mef2 pathway and that this pathway contributes to photoreceptor degeneration in fh mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue by Pdk1/Mef2 knockdown and the activation by sphingolipids.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction and iron toxicity through activation of the sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway synergistically contribute to the demise of neurons in fh mutants.
source: Hence, mitochondrial dysfunction, and iron toxicity through activation of the sphingolipid/Pdk1/Mef2 pathway, synergistically contribute to the demise of neurons in fh mutants.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: Ectopic activation of transcription factor Mef2 induced by loss of FXN may play a role in FRDA.
source: The data indicate that ectopic activation of the transcription factor Mef2 induced by loss of FXN may play a role in FRDA.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the fly model and mammalian cell data.

claim: Mitochondrial mutants in Drosophila that exhibit severely reduced CI activity typically show elevated ROS levels.
source: The lack of increased ROS is surprising as mitochondrial mutants in Drosophila that exhibit a severely reduced CI activity typically show elevated ROS levels (Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008 and Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Several reports have documented that loss of FXN leads to hypersensitivity to ROS, rather than elevated ROS levels.
source: Importantly, several reports have also documented that loss of FXN leads to an hypersensitivity to ROS, rather than elevated ROS levels (Babcock et al., 1997; Llorens et al., 2007; Macevilly and Muller, 1997; Seznec et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Overexpression of ROS scavengers in RNAi mediated fh knock down did not improve viability or cardiac function.
source: Consistent with our data, overexpression of ROS scavengers in an RNAi mediated fh knock down did not improve viability or cardiac function, and no ROS could be detected (Anderson et al., 2005; Shidara and Hollenbeck, 2010; Tricoire et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Loss of Fxn in mice does not lead to an increase in ROS.
source: Similarly, loss of Fxn in mice does not lead to an increase in ROS (Puccio et al., 2001; Seznec et al., 2005), although elevated ROS levels in another mouse model have been documented (Al-Mahdawi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Puccio et al., 2001 and Seznec et al., 2005.

claim: ROS is not a prominent player in FRDA model organisms.
source: Combined, these data suggest that ROS is not a prominent player in model organisms and a clinical trial designed to suppress ROS have not provided compelling data (Santhera Pharmaceuticals, 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the literature and clinical trial data.

claim: Mitochondrial defects are thought to presage iron accumulation in mammals.
source: More importantly, the role of iron in the pathophysiology of FRDA has not yet been determined, and mitochondrial defects are thought to presage iron accumulation in mammals (Puccio et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Puccio et al., 2001.

claim: Fe3+ accumulations are argued to be non-reactive, intra-mitochondrial precipitates.
source: It has been argued that Fe3+ accumulations are a non-reactive, intra-mitochondrial precipitates (Seguin et al., 2010; Whitnall et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seguin et al., 2010 and Whitnall et al., 2012.

claim: In Drosophila fh mutants, both Fe2+ and Fe3+ accumulate in the nervous system.
source: We find that in Drosophila fh mutants, both Fe2+ and Fe3+ accumulate in the nervous system (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by RPA and Perls'/DAB staining data (Figure 3C and D).

claim: Iron accumulation in neurons is toxic and plays a primary role in the pathogenesis in fh mutants.
source: Taken together, we argue that iron accumulation in neurons is toxic and plays a primary role in the pathogenesis in fh mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic and dietary manipulation data.

claim: Sph or dhSph directly induce autophosphorylation of PDK1 or SGK in an in vitro kinase assay.
source: It has been reported that Sph or dhSph, two sphingolipids that are elevated in fh mutants, directly induce autophosphorylation of PDK1 or SGK in an in vitro kinase assay (Caohuy et al., 2014; King et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caohuy et al., 2014 and King et al., 2000.

claim: There is no evidence that PDK1 or SGK can directly activate Mef2.
source: Although there is no evidence that PDK1 or SGK can directly activate Mef2, our data clearly show that Mef2 activity is up-regulated by elevating dhSph in the medium of cultured Neuro-2A cells, and this increased activity is suppressed by a PDK1 inhibitor (Figure 6D), indicating that Mef2 can be activated by PDK1 or a downstream substrate of PDK1 (Mora et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior evidence in the literature.

claim: Mef2 can be activated by PDK1 or a downstream substrate of PDK1.
source: Although there is no evidence that PDK1 or SGK can directly activate Mef2, our data clearly show that Mef2 activity is up-regulated by elevating dhSph in the medium of cultured Neuro-2A cells, and this increased activity is suppressed by a PDK1 inhibitor (Figure 6D), indicating that Mef2 can be activated by PDK1 or a downstream substrate of PDK1 (Mora et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from the luciferase reporter assay data and citation to Mora et al., 2004.

claim: The MEF2 family includes four vertebrate genes (MEF2A–D) that play a key role in muscle differentiation.
source: The MEF2 family includes four vertebrate genes (MEF2A–D) that play a key role in muscle differentiation (Molkentin et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Molkentin et al., 1995.

claim: The MEFs are known to regulate the expression of numerous target genes, including genes required for muscle differentiation, immediate-early genes, neuronal-activity-regulated genes, as well as genes involved in energy storage and immune response.
source: The MEFs are known to regulate the expression of numerous target genes, including genes required for muscle differentiation, immediate-early genes, neuronal-activity-regulated genes, as well as genes involved in energy storage and immune response (Clark et al., 2013; Dietrich, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2013 and Dietrich, 2013.

claim: Ectopic expression of Mef2 in ectoderm is sufficient to induce nearly half of its predicted downstream targets that are typically expressed in muscles.
source: In flies, ectopic expression of Mef2 in ectoderm is sufficient to induce nearly half of its predicted downstream targets that are typically expressed in muscles (Sandmann et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sandmann et al., 2006.

claim: Up-regulation of Mef2 is implicated in cardiac hypertrophy and dilation.
source: Importantly, it has been shown that the up-regulation of Mef2 is implicated in the cardiac hypertrophy and dilation (Molkentin and Markham, 1993; Xu et al., 2006), which is the major cause of death in FRDA patients.
evidence: Supported by citations to Molkentin and Markham, 1993 and Xu et al., 2006.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy and dilation is the major cause of death in FRDA patients.
source: Importantly, it has been shown that the up-regulation of Mef2 is implicated in the cardiac hypertrophy and dilation (Molkentin and Markham, 1993; Xu et al., 2006), which is the major cause of death in FRDA patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FRDA.

claim: Reducing the levels of sphingolipid synthesis with Myriocin, or antisense strategy against enzymes involved in sphingolipid synthesis, or reducing the levels of Pdk1 or Mef2, are options that should be explored in FRDA models.
source: In sum, our data indicate that reducing the levels of sphingolipid synthesis with Myriocin, or antisense strategy against enzymes involved in sphingolipid synthesis, or reducing the levels of Pdk1or Mef2, are options that should be explored in FRDA models.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation based on the study findings.
